cards.front: In a closed population, total growth is the net per-capita rate times size: dN/dt = {{c1::(b − d) × N}}.
cards.back: b and d are per-capita birth and death rates per unit time.
cards.quote: A population's growth is its per-capita rate (births minus deaths per individual, per unit time) times its size: dN/dt = (b − d) × N.

cards.front: When is a population regulated, in terms of its net per-capita growth rate?
cards.back: Only when the net per-capita rate falls as density rises, positive below some level and negative above it, so the population returns to that level from either side (negative density dependence).
cards.why: In real populations this feedback may act after a lag.
cards.quote: A population is regulated only when that net per-capita rate falls as density (individuals per unit area) rises, from positive below some level to negative above it

cards.front: What scope assumptions do both the exponential and logistic models make about the population?
cards.back: One closed population (no immigration or emigration) in a fixed area, so N and density rise together; no age structure; continuous time.
cards.quote: both models describe one closed population (no immigration or emigration) in a fixed area, so N and density rise together, with no age structure and continuous time.

cards.front: What does the exponential model hold constant, and what does the logistic model hold constant and assume about the net per-capita rate?
cards.back: Exponential: b and d constant. Logistic: r and K constant, with b − d falling in a straight line from r at low density to zero at K, and crowding acting at once (no lag).
cards.quote: The logistic holds r and K constant and assumes the net rate b − d falls in a straight line, from r at low density to zero at K

cards.front: With a per-capita birth rate b and death rate d, the intrinsic rate of increase is r = {{c1::b − d}}.
cards.back: r is the per-capita rate when resources are not limiting.
cards.quote: With a per-capita birth rate b and death rate d, r = b − d
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: In population growth models, what are the units of r, and of K?
cards.back: r is per unit time (per day, per year); K is a number of individuals.
cards.why: dN/dt is individuals per unit time and N is individuals, so r must be per unit time for dN/dt = rN to balance.
cards.quote: With a per-capita birth rate b and death rate d, r = b − d: if b = 0.5 per year and d = 0.3 per year, r = 0.2 per year.
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: A population of 50 grows exponentially with constant r = 0.1 per day. Using N(t) = N0 e^(rt), about how many individuals are there at day 10?
cards.back: rt = 0.1 × 10 = 1, e^1 = 2.718, so N(10) = 50 × 2.718 ≈ 136: more than one doubling (100), fewer than two (200).
cards.quote: N(5) = 100 × 2.718, about 272: more than one doubling (200), fewer than two (400).
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: With r = 0.2 per day, the population multiplies by lambda = e^0.2 = 1.22 per day. Why is that a 22% rise, not 20%?
cards.back: r is a net rate acting at every instant, so newcomers start adding newcomers at once; growth compounds within the day.
cards.quote: a 22% rise per day, slightly more than 20% because newcomers start adding newcomers at once.
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: Under exponential growth, over one time unit the population multiplies by lambda = {{c1::e^r}}.
cards.quote: Because r is a net rate (not a birth rate) acting at every instant, over one day the population multiplies by lambda = e^r
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: Show why the exponential doubling time is ln 2 / r.
cards.back: Doubling means e^(rt) = 2. Taking the natural log of both sides gives rt = ln 2 = 0.693, so t = 0.693 / r.
cards.quote: Doubling means e^(rt) = 2; taking the natural log of both sides (ln undoes e; see e and ln) gives rt = ln 2 = 0.693
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: A population grows exponentially with constant r = 0.05 per year. What is its doubling time, and does it change when the population is ten times larger?
cards.back: t = ln 2 / r = 0.693 / 0.05 ≈ 13.9 years. It does not change: a constant r gives a constant doubling time at any N.
cards.quote: With r = 0.2 per day the population doubles every 3.47 days, whether it holds 100 individuals or 100,000.
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: A bacterial culture with unlimited resources rises from 1,000 to 8,000 cells in 6 hours, growing exponentially with constant r. Find the doubling time and r.
cards.back: 8-fold is three doublings, so the doubling time is 6 / 3 = 2 hours. r = ln 2 / 2 = ln 8 / 6 ≈ 0.347 per hour.
cards.quote: A constant r means a constant doubling time, ln 2 / r.
cards.section: A fixed per-capita rate: exponential growth

cards.front: A logistic population has r = 0.3 per day and K = 2,000, with N = 500. Find the brake (1 − N/K) and dN/dt.
cards.back: N/K = 0.25, so the brake is 0.75. dN/dt = 0.3 × 500 × 0.75 = 112.5 individuals per day.
cards.quote: N/K = 0.25, so the brake is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: In the logistic model the per-capita growth rate is (1/N) dN/dt = {{c1::r(1 − N/K)}}.
cards.quote: Divide both sides by N for the per-capita rate: (1/N) dN/dt = r(1 − N/K)
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: In the logistic model, per-capita growth plotted against N is a straight line falling from r through zero at K, the {{c1::carrying capacity}}.
cards.quote: Against N this is a straight line falling from r through zero at K, the carrying capacity
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: Why does total logistic growth dN/dt peak at N = K/2, and what is the peak value?
cards.back: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K) multiplies a size that rises with N by a brake that falls with N; the product is largest at K/2, where it equals rK/4.
cards.quote: Peak total growth. At N = 500, dN/dt = 0.2 x 500 x 0.5 = 50 individuals per day, which is rK/4 = 0.2 x 1,000 / 4.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: In a logistic population with r = 0.2 per day and K = 1,000, N = 100 and N = 900 give the same dN/dt (18 per day). Why?
cards.back: At 100 the per-capita rate is high (0.18) but few individuals carry it; at 900 there are many individuals but the per-capita rate is low (0.02).
cards.quote: At N = 100 and N = 900 the population has the same instantaneous growth rate, dN/dt = 18 individuals per day.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: A logistic population with r = 0.4 per year and K = 500 receives immigrants that raise N to 600. What does the model predict right after, and why?
cards.back: It shrinks back toward K. Per-capita rate = 0.4 × (1 − 1.2) = −0.08 per year, so dN/dt = −48 per year, slowing as N nears 500.
cards.quote: At 1,200 the per-capita rate is 0.2 × (1 − 1.2) = −0.04 per day, so at that moment the population is shrinking at 48 a day
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: Why is K in the logistic model an equilibrium rather than a ceiling?
cards.back: Below K the per-capita rate is positive and above K it is negative, so the population returns to K from either side; it can be pushed above K.
cards.why: From below, the continuous model rises smoothly to K and never overshoots, because feedback is instant.
cards.quote: K is a stable equilibrium, a level the population returns to from either side, not a ceiling.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: Use N(t) = K / (1 + (K/N0 − 1) e^(−rt)) with K = 1,000, N0 = 200, r = 0.5 per day. Find N at day 4, and compare with the exponential projection.
cards.quote: The solution of the logistic equation (you can use it without deriving it) is N(t) = K / (1 + (K/N0 - 1) e^(-rt))
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: For the logistic population with K = 1,000, N0 = 200 and r = 0.5 per day, how long until it reaches K/2?
cards.quote: Taking the natural log of both sides, t = ln 9 / 0.2 = 2.197 / 0.2 = 10.99 days.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: Name three logistic assumptions that field populations break.
cards.back: They have age structure, feedback has time lags, and K changes with season, weather and food supply.
cards.why: These can make a real population overshoot or cycle around K, though none always does.
cards.quote: And K changes with season, weather and food supply.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: Two populations have the same N, but one is mostly juveniles. Which grows more slowly than its N suggests, and why does the logistic model miss the difference?
cards.back: The mostly-juvenile one. Juveniles do not breed; the logistic has no age structure.
cards.quote: Real populations have age structure: juveniles do not breed, so a population of mostly young animals grows more slowly than its N suggests.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: In a deer population, food eaten this winter limits births next spring. Approaching K from below, how can its path differ from the continuous logistic's?
cards.back: It can overshoot K and then oscillate or cycle, because the brake reflects past density; the continuous logistic, with instant feedback, cannot overshoot. A lag makes this possible, not certain.
cards.quote: Feedback has time lags: food eaten this winter limits births next spring.
cards.section: A falling per-capita rate: the logistic model

cards.front: Define a density-dependent factor and a density-independent factor.
cards.back: Density dependent: its per-capita effect changes with density (it tilts the per-capita line). Density independent: shifts the per-capita rate by the same amount at every density.
cards.quote: A density-dependent factor has a per-capita effect that changes with density; it tilts the line.
cards.section: Tilting the line: what counts as a brake

cards.front: How would a field experiment show that food limits a population?
cards.back: Add food to some plots and compare numbers with untouched control plots; if numbers rise with added food, food was limiting there.
cards.quote: if adding food raises numbers compared with untouched control plots, food was limiting there.
cards.section: Tilting the line: what counts as a brake

cards.front: A logistic population has r = 0.3 per day and K = 1,200. A hazard removes 0.1 per individual per day at every density. Does the hazard regulate the population? Where does it settle?
cards.back: It does not regulate. It lowers the per-capita line by 0.1 with its slope unchanged, so zero is crossed where 0.3(1 − N/1,200) = 0.1, at N = 800. The tilt still comes from crowding.
cards.quote: The per-capita line drops by 0.05 at every density with its slope unchanged, so it crosses zero earlier
cards.section: Tilting the line: what counts as a brake

cards.front: A frost kills 30 of 300 hares on a dense plot and 3 of 30 on a sparse plot. It killed ten times more on the dense plot. Is the frost density dependent here?
cards.back: No. The per-capita death rate is 10% on both plots; it kills more in total only because a fixed fraction of a bigger number is bigger.
cards.quote: It kills more in total only because a fixed fraction of a bigger number is bigger.
cards.section: Tilting the line: what counts as a brake

cards.front: Is a predator, or a frost, density dependent by its nature?
cards.back: No. Whether an agent is density dependent is a hypothesis, tested by measuring per-capita rates across densities.
cards.quote: Neither label comes with the agent: whether a predator or a frost is density dependent is a hypothesis, tested on per-capita rates.
cards.section: Tilting the line: what counts as a brake

cards.front: Young reef fish from one generation are stocked at different densities across reefs, and the fraction dying rises with density. Does this show the population is regulated?
cards.back: No. It shows density-dependent deaths in space. Regulation is return through time, which needs long records, repeated density manipulations, or a tested demographic model built from per-capita rates.
cards.quote: Regulation is a claim about return through time, and showing it needs evidence through time
cards.section: What regulates real populations

cards.front: Name two limits of the Kluane snowshoe hare predator-exclusion treatments.
cards.back: Each predator treatment had one fenced block, and fences kept out lynx and coyotes but not birds of prey, so exclusion was partial.
cards.quote: the fences kept out lynx and coyotes but not birds of prey, so exclusion was partial.
cards.section: What regulates real populations

cards.front: In Soay sheep on St Kilda, two populations of equal size under identical winter weather can follow different paths. Which logistic assumption does this break, and how?
cards.back: No population makeup (age and sex classes). Lambs, adult males and adult females respond differently to density and to weather, so the population's makeup changes the outcome; weather and density act together.
cards.quote: lambs, adult males and adult females respond differently to density and to winter weather, so two populations of equal size under identical weather can follow different paths.
cards.section: What regulates real populations

cards.front: A logistic curve fits a country's past census counts closely. Why does this not show that logistic crowding is at work?
cards.back: A close fit to points you already have does not show the equation's mechanism; a model earns trust by predicting populations it was not fitted to.
cards.quote: a close fit to points you already have does not show that the mechanism in the equation is at work.
cards.section: Checking a model against data

cards.front: Ecologists use {{c1::time series}}, counts of the same population year after year, and ask whether a high count is followed by a low per-capita growth rate the next year.
cards.quote: Ecologists use time series, counts of the same population year after year, and ask whether a high count is followed by a low per-capita growth rate the next year.
cards.section: Checking a model against data

cards.front: Many short population time series, each tested alone, give little evidence of density dependence; analysed together they give strong evidence. What is the best interpretation?
cards.back: Low statistical power in short single series, not absent regulation: each series has too little data to detect an effect that is there.
cards.quote: That points to low statistical power in short single series (too little data for a test to detect an effect that is there), not absent regulation.
cards.section: Checking a model against data

cards.front: In a crossed field design, hare density was about 2 times control with mammalian predators excluded, 3 times with food added, and 11 times with both. What do the null expectations and the result suggest?
cards.back: Independent multiplying effects predict 2 × 3 = 6 times; simply adding gains predicts 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 times. Observed 11 exceeds both, suggesting food and predation interact; with one block per predator treatment, this is suggested, not tested.
cards.quote: The observed 11 times exceeds both, which suggests that the two factors interact, as the authors concluded.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Hares reached 11 times control density with food added and mammalian predators excluded. What does this not show, and what should come next?
cards.back: It does not show that food shortage drives the cyclic decline, and density ratios are not r or K. Next: replicate on more blocks, ideally in another region, and measure per-capita survival and reproduction against density in each treatment.
cards.quote: measure per-capita survival and reproduction against density in each treatment
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: With r and K positive, what kind of equilibrium is N = 0 in the logistic model?
cards.back: Unstable: any population above zero grows away from it, while K is stable.
cards.quote: N = 0 is also an equilibrium of the logistic, but unstable: any population above zero grows away from it, while K is stable.
cards.section: Two equilibria

cards.front: A population with an Allee effect is knocked down to very low density. Contrast what the logistic model predicts with what the Allee effect implies.
cards.back: Logistic: per-capita growth is highest near zero, so it recovers. Allee: per-capita growth rises with density at low density, so falling lower slows growth and can push it further from its level.
cards.why: The logistic leaves positive density dependence out.
cards.quote: At very low density the per-capita rate can instead rise as density rises, so the line slopes up before it slopes down.
cards.section: Allee effects

cards.front: Why should a regression of per-capita growth on density from noisy counts be treated with caution?
cards.back: Sampling error in the counts can itself create spurious density dependence; real per-capita lines are also often curved, falling fast at low density then flattening.
cards.quote: sampling error in the counts can itself create spurious density dependence in a regression of growth on density.
cards.section: Real per-capita lines are often curved

cards.front: An insect with one generation per year shows erratic annual counts. A colleague concludes the environment must be erratic. What does the discrete-time logistic say?
cards.back: Not necessarily. With this year's crowding acting on next year's number, a discrete logistic can settle, oscillate or fluctuate chaotically depending on r, with nothing random in the equation.
cards.quote: can settle, oscillate, or fluctuate chaotically depending on r, with nothing random in the equation.
cards.section: Chaos from the simplest model

cards.front: In tests on laboratory Daphnia magna populations, which extinction models predicted extinctions well on populations they were not fitted to?
cards.back: Models letting demographic chance vary with density predicted extinctions accurately or with slight bias; models assuming the same demographic chance at every density were severely biased and underpredicted them.
cards.quote: models that assumed demographic chance was the same at every density were severely biased and underpredicted them.
cards.section: Drake's Daphnia test
